title: Telling stories & real conversation
goal: Tell a story with natural connectors, use relative clauses and reported speech, and sound natural with fillers and idioms.
intro:
Congratulations: you've reached the last unit! Here you'll pull everything together to **tell a story** and handle **real, fast conversation**.

Bengali builds complex sentences in a distinctive way: instead of English 'who/which/where' clauses, it pairs a **relative word (য-)** with a **correlative word (স- / ত-)**: **যে** … **সে** 'the one who … he', **যখন** … **তখন** 'when … then', **যেখানে** … **সেখানে** 'where … there'. Reported speech uses the little word **বলে** ('saying'). And conversation runs on particles and fillers like **তো, মানে, আসলে, আরে, ইয়ে**.

vocab.note: Singular: যে; object: যাকে; possessive: যার. Paired with তারা / ওরা.
Paired with তা 'that': যা বলবে তা করব 'I'll do what you say'.
আমি তো বলেছিলাম! 'But I told you!'
ও নাকি বিয়ে করছে 'apparently he's getting married'.

phrases.en: I was flabbergasted. (lit. 'I fell from the sky')
He/she is hot-tempered. (lit. 'his head is hot')
Don't take it personally. (lit. 'don't rub the words on your body')
To kill two birds with one stone.
Barking dogs seldom bite. (lit. 'it doesn't rain as much as it thunders')
Nonsense! / Nothing at all! (lit. 'a horse's egg')

phrases.native: ও বলল যে ও আসবে না।
phrases.roman: o bollo je o ashbe na.

grammar.title: Relative–correlative sentences: যে…সে, যখন…তখন, যেখানে…সেখানে
grammar.body:
Bengali usually builds 'who/which/when/where' sentences with a **pair** of words: a **relative** (beginning with য-) in the first clause and a matching **correlative** (with স- / ত- / সে-) in the second:

**যে** … **সে** – the person who … (he/she): **যে** ছেলেটা গান গাইছে, **সে** আমার ভাই. 'The boy who is singing is my brother.'
**যিনি** … **তিনি** – respectful
**যা** … **তা** – what … that: **যা** চাও **তা** নাও. 'Take what you want.'
**যখন** … **তখন** – when … then
**যেখানে** … **সেখানে** – where … there
**যেমন** … **তেমন** – as … so
**যত** … **তত** – the more … the more

The correlative can often be dropped in speech, and the relative clause can also come second, introduced by **যে**: এই সেই দোকান, **যেখানে** আমরা প্রথম দেখা করেছিলাম.

examples.native: যে মেয়েটা লাল শাড়ি পরেছে, সে আমার বোন।
examples.roman: je meyeṭa lal shaṛi porechhe, she amar bon.
examples.en: The girl who's wearing the red sari is my sister.

examples.native: যখন আমি ছোট ছিলাম, তখন আমরা ঢাকায় থাকতাম।
examples.roman: jôkhon ami chhoṭo chhilam, tôkhon amra ḍhakay thaktam.
examples.en: When I was little, we lived in Dhaka.

examples.native: যেখানে তুমি যাবে, সেখানে আমিও যাব।
examples.roman: jekhane tumi jabe, shekhane amio jabo.
examples.en: Wherever you go, I'll go too.
The more you learn, the easier it will feel.

grammar.title: Reported speech with বলে and যে
grammar.body:
Bengali reports speech in two ways:

1. **Direct quote + বলে** (*bole*, 'saying'). The original words are kept, including the original person and tense, and **বলে** closes the quote before the main verb: ও বলল, "আমি আসব না" → ও "আসব না" **বলে** চলে গেল 'he left, saying "I won't come"'.
2. **যে** 'that' + the reported clause, usually **keeping the original tense** (unlike English backshifting): ও বলল **যে** ও আসবে না 'he said that he would (lit. will) not come'.

Verbs of thinking work the same way: আমি ভেবেছিলাম **যে** তুমি জানো 'I thought you knew'; ভাবলাম ও রাগ করেছে **বলে** 'I thought (that) she was angry'.

Hearsay uses **নাকি** 'apparently': ও **নাকি** চাকরি ছেড়ে দিয়েছে 'apparently he quit his job'. Questions are reported with **কি** / question words: জিজ্ঞেস করল আমি **কোথায়** থাকি 'asked where I live'.

examples.en: He/she said that tomorrow is a holiday.

examples.native: রাজু আসবে বলে আমরা অপেক্ষা করলাম।
examples.roman: raju ashbe bole amra ôpekkha korlam.
examples.en: We waited because (we were told) Raju would come.

examples.native: উনি জিজ্ঞেস করলেন আমি কোথা থেকে এসেছি।
examples.roman: uni jiggesh korlen ami kotha theke eshechhi.
examples.en: He/she asked where I had come from.
I heard they're apparently moving house.

grammar.title: Sounding natural: particles and fillers
grammar.body:
Fluent Bengali is full of small words that add attitude:

**তো** – emphasis or 'after all': আমি **তো** বলেছিলাম! 'But I *told* you!'; as a starter: **তো**, কী খবর? 'So, what's new?'
**-ই** – 'exactly, only, right': এখন**ই** 'right now', আমি**ই** 'I myself', এটা**ই** 'this very one'.
**-ও** – 'also, even': আমি**ও** 'me too', এখন**ও** 'even now, still'.
**না** at the end of a sentence – softens or asks for agreement: চলো **না**! 'oh come on, let's go!', ভালো, **না**? 'nice, isn't it?'
**মানে** 'I mean', **আসলে** 'actually', **ইয়ে** 'um', **আরে** 'hey / oh', **বাবা!** 'wow!', **ইশ!** 'oh no! / yuck!', **উফ!** 'ugh!', **ব্যস** 'that's it'.

Story connectors: **একদিন** 'one day', **তারপর** 'then', **হঠাৎ** 'suddenly', **তখন** 'at that moment', **শেষে / শেষ পর্যন্ত** 'in the end'.

examples.en: I had no idea at all!
Come on, let's go right now!
I mean, I didn't quite get it.
Two eggs, a bit of bread, that's all!

dialogue.title: A ghost story at the adda
dialogue.setting: Friends are chatting (আড্ডা) on a rainy evening in Kolkata; Shubho tells a story.

lines.speaker: Shubho
lines.native: জানিস, গত বছর আমার সঙ্গে একটা অদ্ভুত ঘটনা ঘটেছিল।
lines.roman: janish, gôto bôchhor amar shôṅge ækṭa ôdbhut ghôṭona ghôṭechhilo.
lines.en: You know, last year something strange happened to me.

lines.speaker: Mili
lines.native: আবার তোর ভূতের গল্প? আচ্ছা, বল।
lines.roman: abar tor bhuter gôlpo? achchha, bôl.
lines.en: Another of your ghost stories? Fine, go on.

lines.speaker: Shubho
lines.native: একদিন রাতে গ্রামের বাড়ি ফিরছিলাম। যেখানে বড় বটগাছটা আছে, সেখানে হঠাৎ আলো নিভে গেল।
lines.roman: ækdin rate gramer baṛi phirchhilam. jekhane bôṛo bôṭgachhṭa achhe, shekhane hôṭhat alo nibhe gælo.
lines.en: One night I was returning to my village home. Right where the big banyan tree is, suddenly the lights went out.

lines.speaker: Shubho
lines.native: দেখি, সাদা শাড়ি পরা এক মহিলা দাঁড়িয়ে আছেন। উনি আমাকে জিজ্ঞেস করলেন আমি কোথায় যাচ্ছি।
lines.roman: dekhi, shada shaṛi pôra æk mohila daṃṛiye achhen. uni amake jiggesh korlen ami kothay jachchhi.
lines.en: I look, and there's a woman in a white sari standing there. She asked me where I was going.

lines.speaker: Shubho
lines.native: আমি তো ভয়ে কাঁপছি! মানে, কিছুই বলতে পারছিলাম না।
lines.roman: ami to bhôye kaṃpchhi! mane, kichhui bolte parchhilam na.
lines.en: I'm shaking with fear! I mean, I couldn't say anything.

lines.speaker: Shubho
lines.native: শেষে উনি হেসে বললেন, "আরে শুভ, আমি তোর পিসি! চিনতে পারছিস না?"
lines.roman: sheshe uni heshe bollen, "are shubho, ami tor pishi! chinte parchhish na?"
lines.en: In the end she laughed and said, "Hey Shubho, I'm your aunt! Don't you recognise me?"

lines.speaker: Mili
lines.native: ঘোড়ার ডিম! যত গর্জে তত বর্ষে না।
lines.roman: ghoṛar ḍim! jôto gôrje tôto bôrshe na.
lines.en: What rubbish! All thunder and no rain.

lines.speaker: Ayan
lines.native: যাই হোক, গল্পটা দারুণ ছিল। আর এক কাপ চা হোক!
lines.roman: jai hok, gôlpoṭa darun chhilo. ar æk kap cha hok!
lines.en: Anyway, it was a great story. Let's have another cup of tea!

culture: The **আড্ডা** — long, unhurried conversation among friends over tea — is a cherished Bengali institution, in Kolkata's College Street coffee house as much as in Dhaka's tea stalls. Ghost stories (ভূতের গল্প) have a whole literary tradition, from Satyajit Ray's tales to the comic ghosts of Upendrakishore. Bengali is rich in proverbs (প্রবাদ); dropping one into conversation, like যত গর্জে তত বর্ষে না, will delight your listeners. You now have the tools to keep learning from real conversation, films, songs and books: শুভকামনা! (Good luck!)
